id_roundabout_boulder.blurb: A single freestanding boulder beside the road near Redfish Lake, south of Stanley in central Idaho, and the biggest cluster of problems in the lake's small bouldering zone. It stands roughly 15 feet tall with lines on three faces and flat ground underneath, so a single pad covers most of it. Thirteen problems run from the easiest grade up to V7, with the bulk in the V1 to V4 range and just a couple of harder outings above that. Quick to reach and easy to combine with other stops around the lake, it suits a short session or a rest-day stroll more than a full day out.

id_12_cannonball_wall.blurb: A small sport wall in the Fins area of central Idaho, one of the crags in the newer Mortal Earth zone, tucked just west of Stone Temple. All thirteen routes are bolted and fall mostly in the 5.7 to 5.9 range, with one at 5.10, making it a handy spot for climbers who want moderates in an area better known for harder lines. The limestone here is peppered with rounded, protruding nodules that make the movement unusual, and the lines feel quite alike. It is a secluded wall and not the quickest to walk to.

id_ball_creek_wall.blurb: A newly developed, little-known cliff in the far north of Idaho, reached by forest road from Bonners Ferry in Boundary County. Locals sometimes call it the Balls Wall. Thirteen routes mix bolted face and slab climbing with a few crack and gear lines, spanning from an easy 5.6 through a solid middle band of 5.9 to 5.11, with one 5.12 and one 5.13 at the top. The upper section sits in shade for most of the day while the lower section catches more sun. Expect a quiet, secluded setting and some lichen and dust on the less traveled lines.

id_playground_the_2.blurb: A vertical basalt wall in Wolverine Canyon east of Firth, within reach of Idaho Falls, sitting downstream from Crank Cave. Thirteen routes, almost all bolted with a single top-rope line, climb blocky, broken rock at grades from about 5.7 to 5.12, with the most routes in the 5.8 to 5.9 band and a few harder lines above 5.10. The canyon turns hot in summer, so climbers favour the early or late parts of the season. The base is reached by a descent trail at the west end near a large pipeline, or you can rappel in from the anchors at the top.
id_playground_the_2.parking_note: Follow Wolverine Canyon Road east out of Firth for around ten miles. If you reach the Rattlesnake transfer sign you have gone about half a mile too far and are at Crank Cave, so turn back and park near the wall.
